title: Clarity vs. Style
principle: Choose the clarity-style balance to fit your game
why: Persona's UI is the most stylish but hard to parse, yet traditional menus would be unwanted; clear UI doesn't always mean good UI, so it depends on what each title demands.
how: Decide early where your UI sits between clarity and style based on the game's content and setting, then improve user-friendliness where you can.
anti_pattern: Assuming the clearest UI is automatically best.
example: Persona series / Persona 5 menus.
quote: In other words, clear UI doesn't always mean good UI, or vice-versa.

title: Clarity vs. Style
principle: Organize menus like a sensible drawer
why: When players pull a menu open they want things organized sensibly; feature-heavy games need drawers on top of drawers, and crafting games leave players drowning in materials.
how: Group related items and plan a window hierarchy proportional to the amount of content and items.
example: Minecraft players build warehouses like their own item folders.
quote: A game's UI is like a drawer. When you pull it open, you want things to be organized in a sensible way.

title: Clarity vs. Style
principle: Review every menu's guidance, size, hierarchy, color and typeface
why: Each menu has key design points: visual guidance, size of display elements, window hierarchy, brightness and saturation, and an appropriate typeface.
how: Use those points as a checklist when designing or reviewing each menu.

title: Name Files Logically
principle: Name player-facing moves in the order players input them
why: In-game it's 'Up Special' because from the player's perspective the directional input comes first, so the name matches how you perform the move.
how: Let in-game move names follow the input sequence, even if internal labels follow a different scheme.
example: Super Smash Bros. 'Up Special' vs. internal 'SpecialHi'.
quote: The name matches how you perform the move.

title: Keeping Rewards in Sight
principle: Show progress toward the next reward and what remains
why: Ys displays current EXP and the amount needed to level up; the number rising with each defeated enemy shows how far you've come and how far is left, which keeps you pushing.
how: Display current versus required values for the next reward on the main screen and update them on every gain.
anti_pattern: Hiding how close the player is to the next reward.
example: Ys (TurboGrafx-16 version) EXP display.
quote: It shows how far you've come, and how far you have left to go. Keeping rewards in sight.

title: Text Size
principle: Size and lay out text per language, not just for English.
why: Kanji need larger characters but fewer of them, English is legible small but runs longer, and French longer still; English-only layouts leave translations too small.
how: Leave flexible room in every text area for each target language's glyph size and string length.
anti_pattern: Designing the layout with only English in mind.
example: Japanese, English and French text compared.
quote: This is something I'd like to impress on developers both in Japan and abroad: the appropriate text size will vary from language to language.

title: Text Size
principle: Check text size on the actual target screen.
why: Handheld developers who check their game on the actual device quickly spot text that's too small, which is why handheld games tend to use larger fonts.
how: Review every UI screen on the real hardware, in each language, during development.
example: Nintendo Switch handheld games.
quote: They'll spot it quickly if the text is too small.

title: Text Size
principle: Offer a player-selectable font size when screen space allows.
why: Letting players choose the font size is extremely accommodating, and a clean interface leaves the screen space to support it.
how: Keep the interface uncluttered and add a font-size setting, while keeping even the largest size reasonably stylish.
anti_pattern: Text so big it no longer looks stylish.
quote: Some games even let you choose the font size for yourself.

title: Modern Quality of Life Features
principle: Let players configure controls freely, with safe remapping
why: Controllers are no longer simple and players arrive with diverse mindsets and experiences; fixed schemes had value mainly for early, simple Nintendo products.
how: Confirm remaps with a long press so short presses still navigate, show each action's default button, allow named profiles, stick swaps and per-context controls (aiming, swimming, menus).
anti_pattern: A fixed, non-remappable control scheme on modern controllers.
example: The Last of Us Part I control menu; named control settings in Smash Bros.
quote: players are coming into these games with diverse mindsets and experiences, so it's necessary to let them set the game up however they like.

title: Modern Quality of Life Features
principle: Show a live preview of what each setting does
why: The right HUD size depends on personal preference and TV setup, and a preview that clearly shows each option's effect is a quality-of-life feature in itself.
how: Add preview windows for HUD options, graphical aids for HUD and reticle choices, dark and bright scenes on brightness/HDR screens, and let players change these mid-game to compare.
example: The Last of Us Part I HUD size preview and HDR brightness screen
quote: It's great how they have this preview window that clearly shows what each option does.

title: Modern Quality of Life Features
principle: Add navigation aids and sensory cues for hard-to-read worlds
why: The player sees only a small part of the world, and the more realistic the game, the harder the environment is to read.
how: Offer optional destination arrows, ledge vibration, audio cues near jump or pickup spots, a screen reader for all text, colorblind and high-contrast modes, and motion-sickness options.
example: The Last of Us Part I Navigation and Traversal, High Contrast Display, Screen Reader
quote: the more realistic a game is, the harder it can be to read the environment, so this can really help.

title: Team Digital or Team Physical?
principle: Let players sort their game libraries into folders
why: For someone who plays lots of games, a way to sort purchases into folders is the thing Sakurai always wants most.
how: In any launcher, storefront or library screen, let users create folders or categories and file their purchases into them.
quote: As someone who plays lots of games, the thing I always want the most is a way to sort my purchases into folders.

title: Loading Screens
principle: Clearly show loading when you can't hide it in presentation
why: Today's players have little interest in waiting, and a wait is easier to accept when the game indicates it is loading.
how: If a load can't be woven into an immersive transition, display a loading indicator right away.
anti_pattern: Silent waits with no indication.
quote: if you're unable to pull that off, I'd say you're better served just clearly stating that the game is loading.

title: Loading Screens
principle: Make loading indicators simple, elegant and true to your world
why: Indicators should be ready to display whenever needed, and plain "Now Loading..." text is rare these days.
how: Design one minimal animated indicator styled after your game's world and use it everywhere.
anti_pattern: Generic "Now Loading..." text.
quote: If you're going to use indicators, try to make them evoke the atmosphere of your game's world!

title: Making Tutorials Feel Natural
principle: Show button prompts that follow the player's remapping
why: Visual control guides have to account for button remapping, so icons must exist for every button the player could use.
how: Drive prompts from the live input mapping and create icons for every possible button.
anti_pattern: Prompts hardcoded to default buttons.
quote: When showing button icons, you need to cover every possible button the player can use.

title: Emphasizing Text
principle: Use text effects to convey emotion in text-heavy games
why: Changing how certain letters or words display conveys a character's emotions and adds flavor, making such effects almost essential.
how: Support inline changes of size, color, animation and font on individual words in your dialogue system.
anti_pattern: One flat text style throughout an expressive, text-heavy game.
example: Japanese comics techniques like kakimoji and manpu.
quote: But changing how certain letters or words are displayed can help better convey a character's emotions or add flavor to an otherwise straightforward presentation

title: Emphasizing Text
principle: Pack expression into limited space with fonts, bubbles and symbols
why: Comic techniques like varied fonts, speech-bubble types and symbols with clear meaning convey emotion concisely.
how: Offer several speech-bubble styles and a few emotion symbols alongside text effects.
example: Manpu such as a sweat bead or vein mark.
quote: And with techniques like changing the font or varying the type of speech bubble, it's possible to pack lots of expression into a relatively limited space.

title: Don't Be Unresponsive
principle: Map menu confirm to more than one button
why: Everyone has their own way of playing, and if L also works as confirm, players can even play one-handed; feeling around for buttons beats unresponsive controls.
how: Accept the main confirm button plus a shoulder button such as L in menus and other UI.
example: Using L as an extra confirm/action button.
quote: For menus and other UI bits, I'd say it's better to have more than one button act as a confirm button.

title: Don't Be Unresponsive
principle: Let button presses during cutscenes bring up a skip prompt
why: Players press buttons because they want something from the game, so cutscenes especially should respond.
how: On any button press during a cutscene, show a prompt that allows skipping.
anti_pattern: Cutscenes that ignore button presses entirely.

title: Menus Define Your World
principle: Use font and UI style to set the world and audience
why: Two games with the same essence and content can target different audiences just by tweaking the UI or font, which is much easier than redesigning characters or environments.
how: Mock up one menu in several styles (slick, cute, horror, flashy, digital, regional) and pick the one that fits your world.
anti_pattern: Treating menus as neutral afterthoughts.
example: Same options screen shown in many styles.
quote: Fonts and UI are both a part of a game's worldbuilding. You might even say they're the package that the world is wrapped in.

title: Menus Define Your World
principle: Keep themed UI legible
why: You want to maintain legibility while proactively designing immersive visuals.
how: Check every themed font and frame for readability at actual screen size before locking it.
anti_pattern: Styling text so heavily it can't be read.
quote: You want to maintain legibility, all while proactively designing immersive visuals.

title: Menus Define Your World
principle: Theme frames, icons, colors and decorations, not just fonts
why: Backgrounds, frames, icons, color choices and decorations all lend the world atmosphere.
how: Style every menu element to match the setting, and choose fonts deliberately even in minimalist designs.

title: Maps Are Game Screens, Too
principle: Design maps so players watch the world, not the corner map
why: When the mini-map holds the player's gaze, the huge, beautifully rendered game screen goes to waste; opening and closing a full map over and over is frustrating.
how: Try a translucent full-screen map overlay usable while playing, with one button to switch to map-only view.
anti_pattern: Making players repeatedly open and close a full-screen map.
example: Mystery Dungeon series: translucent map over the whole screen.
quote: It's important to consider where players will look while they're playing your game. And it's even more important to anticipate what they'll be thinking.

title: Maps Are Game Screens, Too
principle: Put navigation information directly on the game screen
why: On-screen guidance tells players what they need without a glance at the map, as Forza's visual guidance shows how tight a corner is.
how: Add in-world markers or overlays (e.g., cues for upcoming corner sharpness) for the information players would otherwise read off the map.
example: Forza's visual racing guidance.

title: Color-Coding Your Game
principle: Color-code each menu section and carry the color into submenus
why: Pictures and color convey more information than words and are understood through intuition, while text has to be read before it's understood.
how: Assign each top-level menu a color (Smash: red, Spirits: green) and theme all its submenus to match; use large images on panels.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate main menu.
quote: Compared to text, pictures can be recognized much faster, and parsed largely through intuition.

title: Color-Coding Your Game
principle: Avoid a mishmash of colors on a single screen
why: Mixing many colors on one screen often results in a mess, depending on design quality and direction.
how: Keep one dominant color theme per screen; large character art can be the exception, since the images become memorable.
anti_pattern: A jumble of competing colors on one screen.
example: Smash for 3DS/Wii U's character-art panels mixed colors but stayed readable.

title: Color-Coding Your Game
principle: Let the game's tone decide how much color the UI uses
why: Lots of color can make a game feel aimed at younger audiences; any color choice works if it matches the game's atmosphere.
how: Choose palette saturation to fit your tone and audience before applying color-coding.
anti_pattern: Applying bright color-coding regardless of the game's tone and manner.

title: Make Important Elements Bigger
principle: Size menu items by how often players use them
why: Size shows which modes take priority, so players reach the most-used options fastest. It's all about ease of access.
how: Rank menu options by expected use and make the top ones the largest tiles or icons, shrinking rarely used ones.
anti_pattern: Presenting every option as an equal-weight list when some matter far more.
example: Menus from Meteos onward, including the Smash Bros. menu.
quote: The size indicates which modes take priority and what's important.

title: Make Important Elements Bigger
principle: Test icon menu layouts against wider languages early
why: Icon menus are hard to fit in languages that take more horizontal space. The Smash layout worked best in Japanese.
how: Mock up icon labels in your longest target language before locking the layout.
anti_pattern: Designing labels for one language and leaving translation to squeeze in later.
example: Smash Bros. menu translations.

title: I Want to Choose Fast!
principle: Make menu selection fast; cut the steps to the player's choice
why: Of all game inputs, menu selection is what Sakurai most wants to be quick; a scroll wheel would let him zip right to his choice instead of tapping repeatedly.
how: Count inputs to the most common menu choices and reduce them; support D-pad navigation rather than repeated stick taps.
anti_pattern: Menus that require tap-tap-tapping the analog stick.
example: Nintendo GameCube / Smash Bros. Melee — scroll wheel suggestion
quote: A scroll wheel would let me zip right to my choice and be done in a flash.

title: I Want to Choose Fast!
principle: Give menu navigation a clicky, tactile step
why: Games are about play, so tactile 'clicky' feedback, like a notched wheel or a D-pad, makes even selection feel more immersive.
how: Make each step of menu movement distinct and crisp so scrolling feels physical.
example: D-pad vs. analog stick in menus
quote: Games are about play, so that tactile feedback would make gameplay feel more immersive.

title: I Want to Choose Fast!
principle: Treat every new input device as a chance to improve UI
why: Sakurai re-examines things taken for granted and has approached new devices as UI opportunities ever since designing Melee.
how: When a platform adds an input such as a wheel, touch or gyro, prototype using it to speed up selection.
example: Super Smash Bros. Melee era hardware suggestions
quote: But new devices are new opportunities!

title: I Want to Choose Fast!
principle: Layer shortcuts over a beginner-friendly path; don't depend on them
why: The more advanced the shortcut options, the less inexperienced players use them, and the UI can lose broad appeal, so it's a tough line to walk.
how: Keep a simple default way through every menu and add shortcuts as optional accelerators for experienced players.
anti_pattern: Expert-only shortcut systems as the main way to navigate.
quote: Still, the more advanced your shortcut options, the less inexperienced players will use them, and you may end up with a UI that lacks broad appeal

title: The Pros and Cons of Leaderboards
principle: Express rank so improvement raises the number, not a position
why: Ordinary leaderboards tell anyone below first that they're losing, and 400th or x-millionth place saps motivation; GSP measures power against the global player count, so higher is better.
how: Show standing as how many players someone is above, computed against total population, instead of a position where lower is better.
anti_pattern: Raw position leaderboards for huge player bases.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate — Global Smash Power (GSP)
quote: In other words, unlike a leaderboard where the lower number is better, this system says that the higher number is better.

title: Let Them Skip, Let Them Pause
principle: Make every non-interactive sequence skippable, all at once
why: Not being able to skip video content is flat-out inconvenient, and a player without save data may still have seen it before.
how: Allow a single press to skip company logos, opening movies, intermissions and cutscenes, even on a fresh save; let in-engine dialogue advance line by line.
anti_pattern: Forcing players to watch because you want them to see everything you made.
quote: When the player's not in control, make sure they can skip what you're showing them—I can't emphasize that enough.

title: Let Them Skip, Let Them Pause
principle: Let players pause during cutscenes
why: Phone calls, visitors or dinner can pull players away at any moment, and skip-only cutscenes aren't modern design.
how: Support pausing mid-cutscene everywhere except in online games that keep advancing.
anti_pattern: Cutscenes that can be skipped but not paused.

title: Let Them Skip, Let Them Pause
principle: Write logo guidelines that assume logos are skippable
why: Unskippable logos imposed by company guidelines or regulations aren't popular nowadays.
how: If you set company or platform logo rules, make skippability the default.

title: Customization Lets Your Imagination Play
principle: Show customization effects visually instead of with numbers alone
why: Customization feels like a chore unless players can see what their work will result in, and numbers alone are less intuitive.
how: Draw the attack range or other effect directly on the customization screen when a part is selected.
anti_pattern: Showing attack power differences only as numbers.
quote: In games like these, the work players put into customization is a big part of the appeal— so it's imperative that the work itself is fun.

title: Customization Lets Your Imagination Play
principle: Make picking parts fast with sorting, distinct icons and auto-equip
why: Lots of items is good for collectibles, but players accumulate so much that selection becomes slow and similar icons cause struggle.
how: Add sorting and categories, keep every icon visually distinct, and include an automatic equip-strongest option.
anti_pattern: Look-alike icons and unsorted inventories.

title: Button Settings
principle: Ship a key config in every game, however simple
why: Button settings are a necessity for some players, and consoles don't yet offer per-game remapping; console-wide remaps affect every game and can leave actions unmapped.
how: Build an in-game button settings screen and make sure no action can end up without a button.
anti_pattern: Leaving remapping to a console-wide setting.
example: Switch's console-wide remap applies to all applications.
quote: However, it's a necessity for some of our players. Whenever possible, I urge you to add support for this feature.

title: Button Settings
principle: Show the controller graphically and assign buttons with a cursor
why: Vertical lists make it hard to track which button does what, and press-to-assign screens can capture the menu's own exit button.
how: Draw the controller, let players select a button with the cursor, then choose its action from a list.
anti_pattern: A vertical list with press-the-button assignment.
example: Smash Bros. depicts all controllers graphically.

title: Button Settings
principle: Allow shared actions and portable control profiles
why: Smash Bros. is played together, so guest players need a fast way to load their controls.
how: Let multiple buttons map to one action, save layouts under profile names selectable before a fight, and store them on the controller when possible.
example: Smash Bros. has two jump buttons and name-based control profiles.

title: Presenting Scores
principle: Count score gains up point by point so they feel better
why: Even a conventional score deserves careful presentation, and showing the increase step by step can make that part of the design feel even better.
how: Animate each score award as a running tally instead of snapping the total straight to its new value.
quote: I'd also consider things like showing the score increase point-by-point to potentially make that aspect of the game's design feel even better.

title: Advancing Text
principle: Let players speed through text and skip dialogue line by line
why: People read quickly and zipping through text feels good, and everyone wants to enjoy as much as possible in as little time, as video playback-speed settings show.
how: Let a button press complete and advance text immediately, and in cutscenes add a skip that jumps to the start of the next line.
anti_pattern: Forcing everyone through text and scenes at one slow pace.
example: Some games let you skip dialogue one line at a time, jumping to the start of the next line.
quote: Hence, by making dialogue skippable as much as possible, you may just be making a great number of players happy.

title: Advancing Text
principle: Let players listen to dialogue while they keep playing
why: Detailed cutscene performances can't move at the speed players want, and letting dialogue play during gameplay means players don't have to stop and wait.
how: Deliver story or conversation as voiced lines during gameplay instead of pausing play for them.
quote: Or, make it so that people can listen to the dialogue while they play.

title: Adding Help Text to Menus
principle: Never explain a menu item using the item's own name
why: Help text exists for players who don't know what the term means, so repeating the name misses the point, and Sakurai says it happens quite often.
how: Rewrite with different words: "Options" becomes "Adjust a variety of game settings."
anti_pattern: Help text like "Go to the Options."
quote: This is important, so I'll say it again: don't explain using the same words!

title: Adding Help Text to Menus
principle: Polish help text and mode names down to their plain meaning
why: Being immediately clear in a few words is hard, so you must drill down to the most important part, and not everyone knows technical terms.
how: Cut excess words, translate meaning rather than words, prefer "Play Solo" over "1P Mode", and replace terms like "config" or "key repeat".
anti_pattern: Technical terminology in menus.

title: Adding Help Text to Menus
principle: Add help text to menus proactively
why: Menu items are usually one or two words that often don't say what they do; Sakurai considers help text relatively vital and has used it in almost all his games.
how: Show a one-line description of the highlighted item, for example at the bottom of the screen.

title: Making Things Clear, Even Without Words
principle: Make menus usable without reading any text
why: Pictures on icons are more fun to look at and help players work out what each one does, even in a language they can't read.
how: Add a picture or character to each major menu icon, then test the menus in a language you can't read.
anti_pattern: Text-only menus that become unusable without the language.
example: With the menus switched to Korean, the pictures on each icon still help comprehension somewhat.
quote: Ideally, games should be playable even if you can't read a single word.

title: Making Things Clear, Even Without Words
principle: Let repeated confirm presses lead straight into the main game
why: A player who can't read anything can still start playing, and Sakurai sets this up on purpose rather than leaving it to chance.
how: Set default cursor positions from the title screen onward so mashing confirm reaches the main mode, tutorial included.
example: Smash Bros. Ultimate reaches Smash mode's fighter select, Kirby Air Ride the first Air Ride stage, and Kirby Super Star the first scenario with tutorial.

title: CRT Displays
principle: Keep essential information inside the visible safe area
why: On CRTs only about 490 of 525 scanlines were usable and the whole image was never visible, so developers assumed the edges would never be seen.
how: On any display that may crop the image, leave margins at the edges and keep important elements out of them.
example: NES-era games, where scrambled characters at the screen edge weren't a problem because no one saw them.
quote: On a CRT display, you can't see the entire screen.

title: HUDs
principle: Auto-hide or fade HUD elements that would obstruct play
why: A HUD is useful but can crowd the screen, and player cursors would be an eyesore if always visible.
how: Hide cursors based on distance and situation, and make HUD panels semi-transparent when a character overlaps them.
anti_pattern: Always-visible markers cluttering the play area.
example: Smash Bros. player cursors and semi-transparent HUD.
quote: These would be a real eyesore if they were always visible, so they're made to automatically hide themselves based on distance and situation.

title: HUDs
principle: Use the HUD to add character appeal and energy
why: Fighters are sometimes small on screen, so faces turned toward the audience boost appeal, and upward-scrolling patterns suggest burning spirit.
how: Put character portraits facing the player in the HUD, and animate their backgrounds with UV scrolling rather than a flat, static image.
example: Smash Bros. HUD from Brawl onward.
quote: The fighters are sometimes quite small on-screen— so this helps boost their character appeal.

title: HUDs
principle: Make HUD elements react to game state and surface hard-to-track info
why: In 3D it's hard to know how many opponents you've damaged, and meters that change or break make the HUD informative and fun to look at.
how: Swap meters per ability, break them when the vehicle is destroyed, and show icons for opponents you've hit or defeated.
example: Kirby Air Ride's ability meters and opponent icons; Meteos' alien head spinning faster with the Speeder.
quote: In a 3D space, it can be difficult to know how many opponents you've dealt damage to, but I'd say this is an effective solution.
